comment_text.value:
It's interesting that he brings up Diablo 2 and Diablo 3 (and Quake for that matter), though, because I think it really foregrounds why these discussions are so fraught.

I worked in early AAA in the late 90s, and it's true that games were often quite rough around the edges. But they were also often biting off WAY more than they could chew, inventing genres and innovating like crazy, often in messy ways that didn't always work. But that meant players were often also routinely and genuinely surprised by the experiences they encountered in even big budget games.

He lists a bunch of quality of life and balance issues that were fixed in Diablo 3 compared to Diablo 2... but, well, Diablo 2 was obviously _important_ in ways that Diablo 3 wasn't. It's a much greater game.

And lurking in the background is the hard fact that often the progress with software (certainly game software) entailed turning to much better software engineering standards, using much better external libraries or game engines with much larger teams, and relying on much more process to capture and filter all those rough edges... and along the way, you've built a much, much larger team with a much larger burn rate, and so all those experiments and innovations become much more dangerous and need to be corralled and controlled and mostly stifled, and as the cost of all this to build skyrockets your entire game design _has_ to focus on your business model and your microtransaction story and your live services first and foremost, because you've boxed yourself into a corner where that cash flow issue is the central fact of your game / software design.

(I experienced this evolution first hand in the FPS space)

All of which is to say, I think there are multiple different axes at play here for evaluation, and it's probably fair to say that software _undefinably_ was much worse in the past along some of them... but not all of them. And there are probably deep tensions and tradeoffs between some of those axes.

I think this entirely discussion really is muddied, though, too, by the fact that hardware got radically better over this entire arc as well, and so many programming techniques in the past that made software more brittle or crash prone hinged on memory and computation optimizations techniques that really had nothing to do with the software culture of then or now. It was just a response to the realities of the hardware.

story_title.value: Software may be getting worse, but it used to be horrible

"AI skills" are the same skills we always needed:

- Learning in a self-directed way that aligns with the needs of your role and where it is going

- Clear communication, the ability to edit and know how to say what is important

- Forming and testing hypotheses

- Evaluating and testing tools and work product, and being able to recognize and rectify deviations

- Delegating, setting constraints, rubrics and escalation criteria

- Having a clear definition of done and being able to stick with it

- Understanding business domains and modelling them usefully

- Collaborating with others, communicating your needs and capabilities clearly, eliciting the needs and capabilities of others, synthesizing conflicting needs and aligning compounding capabilities

The adoption of genAI and agentic tooling really just serves to make all of these more important.

comment_text.value:
I say that hardware design has a way bigger solution space.

In chess, being able to check hundreds of lines per second makes you a superhuman. But in hardware design you get lost if you try to search the solution space for a circuit, schematic, component selection, layout, routing, stiffener and thermal solution.

There are a few like positioning and routing where the solution space can just be considered infinite as there are infinite copper geometries (even if you stick with straight line polygons) that can connect a number of infinitely differently positioned components.

Then, for the mechanical stiffener, again you have an infinite number of geometries that don't clash with your components, don't run over your copper traces and make the board resist the mechanical tests (which the AI could check with a lengthy FEM analysis per iteration).

After all that, or in parallel with the mechanical analysis you can run the thermal ones and tweak positions of the hot stuff and thickness of stiffener walls to get everything fine.

I just can't see an LLM do that with a board with a few hundred components, even if most are decoupling capacitors.

story_title.value: Superhuman Hardware Design Is the Easy Part

comment_text.value:
I have to disagree here. While it's been proven that a lot of things can be done by just searching a very big solution space very fast (either by brute compute or by a sophisticated algo or both), hardware solution spaces are not that easily searched.

For a lot of applications where signal integrity is not critical, high frequency switching is not required and power density is moderate, yeah. Anyone can do that, even an AI. But you don't even need to make a pcb for those cases, just throw the components in a protoboard and fire away.

When you start adding variables to the search space (emi interference, matching routing impedances, heat management, mechanical integrity, etc) the search space grows so big that any non-expert will become lost in it.

Will future cheap compute power be able to overcome this? I'm not betting on it.

comment_text.value:
I’m well aware that Reddit doesn’t reflect reality. Most of society is not far left, chronically online, violent, and out of touch with reality.

The study you provide isn’t related to my comment but if you’d like to shoehorn it into future discussions you should at least read it first. That paper is widely criticised, and is, ironically, the kind of thing shared on Reddit. I’ll just copy and paste existing academic criticisms of the paper because I don’t really think you’re going to take the time to seek this out yourself.

1. Inconsistent data collection: The far-right data came from an established extremism database, while the far-left data had to be assembled separately because the database did not routinely track most far-left extremism. This creates a potential sampling bias, with no demonstrated guarantee that both sides received equally comprehensive coverage.

2. Serious numerical inconsistencies: The study counts 168 deaths from the Oklahoma City bombing but reports zero far-right bombing incidents. It also contains basic arithmetic errors, including percentages totalling 110%. These inconsistencies raise legitimate concerns about data quality and the reliability of the analysis.

3. Subjective ideological classifications: The study uses broad political definitions and includes homicides with weak evidence of ideological motivation. Without a fully accessible case-level audit trail, independent researchers cannot easily verify whether incidents were classified consistently or accurately.

4. Unsupported statistical conclusions: The author suggests far-left attacks are more likely to cause multiple fatalities, but the reported difference is not statistically significant (Fisher's exact test, p ≈ 0.22). Drawing substantive conclusions from this difference is therefore questionable.

5. Disproportionate influence of one attack: The Oklahoma City bombing accounts for approximately 32% of all far-right fatalities in the study. Removing that single incident reduces the far-right-to-far-left fatality ratio from 6.7:1 to 4.6:1. The overall disparity remains, but its magnitude is significantly influenced by one exceptional event.

6. Selective historical timeframe: The study begins in 1990, excluding the 1960s–1980s, when far-left revolutionary movements were especially prominent in American domestic terrorism. This timeframe may be appropriate for the research question, but it makes broad claims about political violence across modern history misleading.

7. Conclusions beyond the evidence: The study examines ideologically motivated homicides, not political violence generally. It excludes non-fatal assaults, riots, intimidation, arson without fatalities and other violent offences. Using its findings to claim that the far-right is responsible for most actual violence is therefore a substantial and unjustified extrapolation.

Notably, the time frame used doesn’t reflect reality today, so it cannot be used to make normative claims about which ideology is more violent right now.

comment_text.value:
You can try open models via OpenRouter and omp without having to buy or rent any GPU. I routinely try open models to see where they are. GLM 5.3 with DSFV4.1 as advisor via omp feels Opus 4.6 level, i.e. totally able to ship stuff.

I do use Anthropic and OpenAI mostly because it costs me 1/40 and 1/50 of the api prices, which is way cheaper than Chinese subscriptions, but I’m ready to jump ship when they pull the plug. Fortunately they have nothing that forces me to keep paying them, and I don’t pay the crazy enterprise subscription costs, just the personal account prices.

I also die to be able to run the OSS setup locally to stop being spied on all the time.

For context, I averaged 10 hours a day prompting LLMs from when ChatGPT came out. At the start it was just function generation, then single file modules, then modules, and now I reason, design, implement and test with them.

An interesting thing is that with omp you can plan with a smart model and then implement with a dumber one. So for example, plan with Kimi 3.1 via OpenRouter and then implement with DSFV4 with zero data retention active, sorted by cheapest, and minimal tps accepted.

I get the people who are pissed about their cushy jobs evaporating, but if you know how to use these technologies it’s very freeing because it’s like having a company of people working for you, except they are not human so they’re not wasting their life working for you instead of using it for themselves.

You can make them do pretty much everything that is fuzzy-verifiable, you don’t have to worry about their feelings or that they won’t do what you asked them to do or stop, and you can activate them when you want at scale in parallel or not use them at all for days.

For me it’s a dream honestly. I never felt so much empowered in my life while being enabled to unlock my creativity with almost no boundaries.

comment_text.value:
With ChatGPT, I notice it tends to use abstract subjects. E.g., ChatGPT wrote "Texas allows treated sewage sludge to be used as agricultural fertilizer, yet the proposed law requiring routine PFAS testing failed to advance". I would have written "Texas allows treated sewage sludge to be used as agricultural fertilizer, yet the state failed to advance the proposed law requiring routine PFAS testing".

No matter how many times, I ask it to avoid fluff; it keeps writing it. E.g., Please avoid fluff sentences like "This is where the story gets more interesting." and "Here is how the evidence compares." They are not needed and serve no purpose.

I also notice its sentences do not provide a clear sense of who did what. E.g., it wrote "According to pilgrimage organizer Christian Marquant, Bishop Schneider met with Pope Leo in December 2025 and discussed the traditional Latin Mass." I would have wrote "According to pilgrimage organizer Christian Marquant, Bishop Schneider discussed the traditional Latin Mass with Pope Leo on December 2025." The phrase "met with" was extraneous and made it seem like the meeting was by accident.

story_title.value: Why is AI generated language so hard to understand?

comment_text.value:
Operating a Go gateway in production (single machine, ~20B tokens/month across several upstreams), usage-reporting quirks are exactly where our pain concentrated too. What survived for us:

- Treat every upstream try as an attempt with its own usage record, and let request cost be whatever the attempts sum to. Without attempt-level accounting, retries make your per-request numbers lie: you count the first attempt's tokens but pay for the retry. - Vendor-reported usage is advisory, not gospel. Some providers emit usage only on the final SSE chunk, some want stream_options, some never report it for streams at all. The parser zoo is unavoidable, but the damage is contained if the rest of the system treats usage as best-effort telemetry. - The sneaky case is disconnects, not usage: a client disconnect storm once looked identical to backend failures and put every healthy backend into cooldown until the pool was empty. Disconnects are network, not backend health - classifying them separately bought us more than any routing policy change.

How does Respan handle the retry-accounting side - do plugins see per-attempt records, or is usage aggregated at the request level after middleware runs?

story_title.value: Launch HN: Respan (YC W24) – Open-source Rust AI gateway built around plugins

(Card carrying time-nuts member here.)

Yes, I used to have two Cesium standards in my basement, and that allowed me to make FreeBSD the first kernel which could be wrangled to nano-seconds.

These days timekeeping is much more routine and standard hardware, but even if you miss out on LORAN-C and time-by-telephone and leap-seconds, it can still be lots of fun.

Once you get into it, you can look at the log files, call the remote site, and tell them that somebody left the door to the server room open again.

How ?

A temperature difference of 1°C more or less translates to a 1PPM shift (one microsecond per second) in the kind of crystals used for modern motherboard clock chains.

Most air-con systems will oscillate a couple of degrees with approx 20minute period (gentlemen: Tune your PLLs), so a sudden 5 PPM excursion is either a broken air-con or a door left open.

One of the most amazing feats of applied time-nuttery was Steven J. Murdochs work on fingerprinting the timezone of remote servers, based on their TCP sequences numbers.

(Amongst other things, he found out that a lot of Tor nodes were most probably located in north-eastern USA.)

https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1180405.1180410

comment_text.value:
It's a blurry line. When you replace the deck of "bad stuff happens" cards in a solo game with an app that reads them out to you, but the app could have been a deck of cards, which side of the line does that land? What about if the app starts tracking game state for you as well? Game state that could have been tracked with moving tokens around the board, or using dice as counters, but is simpler in the app. Does that cross the line into video-game territory? What if the app tracks hidden game state, doing the job a human GM would need to do. Does that cross the line?

It's very, very fuzzy. Which may be part of why some board game designers chose not to create companion apps. For example, Arydia (designed by Cody Miller and Ira Fay) tracks game state with three large boxes of playing cards, some of which have "B" and "C" versions; the game will routinely tell you that after you defeat such-and-such an enemy, switch NPC-32 into the "B" state. So you take the NPC-32A card out of the active section of the box and put it in the inactive section, and take the NPC-32B card out of the inactive section and put it in the active section. That could have been done with an app, but every time the question of a companion app gets raised on the Arydia forums at BoardGameGeek, the game designers say "We thought about doing an app, but decided it didn't fit with our vision for the game; we wanted it to be purely a board game with physical components." (I'm paraphrasing rather than quoting).

By the way, I highly recommend Arydia if you're into board games with an exploration, adventuring experience. It's the game that has come closest of all the ones I've played to "RPG campaign in board game form". It's got a steep price because of all the physical components included in the game. But my word, is it worth the price if that kind of gameplay is up your alley (and it is very much up mine). You'll get hours and hours of gameplay out of it, and when you're done, you can reset the campaign and play again. You might think "Oh, I'll remember everything from my first playthrough" but the game is long enough that you probably won't remember most of it.

Anyway, enough rambling about one of only 3-4 games I ever rated 10/10 on BGG. We were discussing board game "companion apps", and there are definitely some that I would say "Yeah, that's a video game in board game shape". But I don't buy those, they don't appeal to me, so I really don't remember their names. They definitely exist, though.

Just changing one statement requires new verification, which is why formally verified code currently is not touched but ported verbatim into new projects and “rewrites”. That cost may decrease, which is nice but also not nice: the systems you currently want to formally verify are systems you might not want to alter without high friction in the first place.

I’m hopeful it will produce more robust software, and I’m by no means against it, but I’m skeptical of producing more when we might want to produce less.

I put my list on the mirror in the bathroom, right in front of my face, to try to build a morning routine. I got sick of forgetting to brush my teeth, or put on deodorant, etc. That list sat on my mirror for 2 years, and every morning I would forget to use it. Fuck I hate it.

I had 3 therapists I went through. After the first few meetings where they tell you you have ADHD, they all eventually stopped being helpful. Mostly I needed them to tell me what I needed to do to to build good habits or what I can do to work around my ADHD... and all they wanted to do was listen to me talk and provide no helpful information. None of them told me about the side effects of the medication, how I should use it, or anything. Now I have no therapist, and I'm not really any worse off. The medication helped me way more. But that's just my experience.
